chapters.title: Give Responsibility for Disruptive Technologies to Organizations Whose Customers Need Them

chapterBreakdown.gentle: A disruptive effort can be judged more fairly if it lives in the right organization. Chapter 6 says the right home is the unit whose customers actually need the new technology. If the effort sits inside a group whose existing customers do not care about it, that group has little practical reason to make it central. Leaders may say it matters, but everyday priorities will still follow the customers already funding the business. The chapter's point is structural. Organizations respond to customer pull, not only to executive wishes. That is why separate or autonomous responsibility can matter. It changes which customers define success. The rule is not that every new effort must become a separate company. The rule is that customer fit should decide where responsibility belongs.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Part 2 now turns toward organization placement. A disruptive technology should be managed by the organization whose customers need it, not automatically by the incumbent unit that leads the current business. If the wrong unit owns the effort, the project can look important in speeches and still lose every real resource contest. The reason is structural. Organizations learn priorities from the customers they serve. When those customers do not need the disruptive technology, the unit will keep treating it as secondary. Separate responsibility matters because it can place the effort under a customer logic that gives it a real reason to grow.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: The wrong home can kill a disruptive effort even after the company notices it. Put the project inside a unit whose customers do not need it, and that unit will keep serving the people who made it successful in the first place. The effort gets translated into the old customer's language, then trimmed until it fits the old game. Chapter 6 names the fix sharply: responsibility belongs with the organization whose customers actually want the new technology. Autonomy matters here because it changes who gets a vote. The rule is not 'split everything apart.' It is 'stop housing the future with customers who do not need it.'

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Once managers stop asking a disruptive effort to pass the old business case too early, another question becomes unavoidable: who should actually own the work? Chapter 6 answers that responsibility belongs with the organization whose customers need the disruptive technology.

That rule matters because organizations do not prioritize issues in the abstract. They are shaped by the customers they already serve. Those customers define what counts as urgent, profitable, and worth improving. If the disruptive effort sits in a unit whose current customers do not want it, the unit will keep finding reasonable grounds to give other things priority.

This is why the problem is structural rather than personal. Leaders inside the incumbent unit may be intelligent, sincere, and even sympathetic to the disruptive idea. Yet their daily commitments still run through the customers who justify the unit's budget and status. The project can be treated as important in principle while remaining marginal in practice.

The chapter's response is to place responsibility where customer pull exists. Separate or autonomous responsibility matters because it can align the effort with a group whose success depends on serving the market that actually values the new technology. That creates a fairer environment for learning, commitment, and growth.

The limit remains important. The chapter is not saying every disruptive effort should be spun out completely or that structure solves everything by itself. Its narrower claim is that customer fit should govern organizational placement. Without that fit, competence can still produce rational neglect.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The Part 2 response sharpens here into an organizational rule. A disruptive technology should be given to the organization whose customers need it. If the incumbent unit's customers do not care about the new technology yet, that unit is structurally unlikely to make the project central no matter how much leadership says it matters.

The reason is that customer demand shapes priorities inside an organization. Budgets, attention, and improvement efforts follow the people whose needs define success. A project owned by the wrong unit therefore gets filtered through the wrong customer logic. It can be redirected, delayed, or thinned out in perfectly rational ways.

Executive intention is not enough. Leaders can order support, but the unit still lives inside a system of customers, revenue expectations, and prestige signals that reward the established business. The project is not ignored because the managers are foolish. It is under-served because the organization is built to answer to different demand.

Christensen's response is not generic decentralization. It is customer-fit placement. Separate or autonomous responsibility matters only because it can place the disruptive technology inside a group whose customers create a real reason to care. The aim is to give the effort a home where success is measured by the people who need it, not by the people who would rather preserve the old trajectory.

That keeps the chapter precise. Placement is not the whole answer to disruption, but it is a necessary answer to the problem of rational neglect inside the wrong unit.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A brutal follow-up to Chapter 5 appears here: if the old business grades the new effort badly, who gets the case next? Christensen's answer is sharp. Give responsibility to the organization whose customers actually need the disruptive technology.

This is not an org-chart preference. It is a demand-side rule. Organizations do not chase priorities evenly. They chase the customers who pay for relevance, budget, and status. Put the disruptive effort inside a unit whose customers do not want it, and the unit will keep serving the people who made it strong. The project may stay alive on paper and still lose every serious contest.

Goodwill is not enough. Competent managers can support the idea in words while starving it in practice because the real pressure comes from a different customer set. The wrong home keeps translating the new effort into the old market's priorities until the disruption is trimmed into something safe and secondary.

Separate responsibility matters because it can change who counts as the judge. A unit whose customers need the new technology has a live reason to improve it, defend it, and build around it. Autonomy is doing one job here: shifting whose demand controls the work.

The chapter still has a limit. It does not say every disruptive move belongs in a fully separate company. It says customer fit should decide the home's legitimacy. Without that, smart management can still suffocate the future.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A second structural correction follows Chapter 5's grading problem. Even if managers stop demanding the incumbent business's proof too early, a disruptive effort can still fail if it is housed inside the wrong organization. The ownership question gets a demand-side rule here: give responsibility to the organization whose customers need the disruptive technology.

That rule is necessary because organizations do not operate by intention alone. They are shaped by the customers they already serve. Those customers define what counts as urgent, profitable, prestigious, and worth improving. If the disruptive technology matters little to them, the incumbent unit can support the effort rhetorically while still giving its real energy to something else.

This makes the problem structural rather than moral. The incumbent team may be capable, disciplined, and even curious. Yet its budget logic, planning cadence, and performance standards are all tied to customers who reward the established trajectory. Under those conditions, the disruptive effort is repeatedly translated into a language that weakens it. The unit does not have to hate the new technology to be the wrong home for it.

Executive sponsorship does not solve the issue by itself. Senior leaders can announce that the disruptive project matters, but the owning organization still answers every day to customers whose needs keep scoring higher. Attention, talent, and improvement flow toward the demand system that already pays for legitimacy.

Chapter 6 therefore pushes toward separate or autonomous responsibility, but only for a precise reason. Autonomy matters when it allows the disruptive effort to be judged by customers who genuinely need it. The move is meant to align ownership with demand so the initiative can be prioritized on its own terms.

The chapter's hard contradiction is that a strong incumbent organization can produce rational neglect. Competence, discipline, and good process do not rescue the effort if the unit's customer base keeps telling it that the disruptive technology is marginal. The wrong home can turn underinvestment into common sense.

The limit is equally important. Christensen is not saying that every disruptive effort requires a standalone company or that structure alone resolves the rest of Part 2. The narrower claim is that customer-fit placement is a necessary precondition for fair evaluation and sustained commitment.

Chapter 6 leads naturally into Chapter 7. Once the effort sits with customers who need it, the next question is whether the organization is sized so that the market can matter enough to it. First get the right home. Then ask whether the home's scale matches the market's scale.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The management response now becomes an organizational rule. If a disruptive technology is placed inside an organization whose customers do not need it, that organization is structurally unlikely to make the effort central. The chapter's answer is therefore to give responsibility to the organization whose customers do value the new technology.

The mechanism is demand-driven. Organizations learn priorities from the customers that define their success. Those customers shape budgets, improvement targets, planning rhythms, and standards of seriousness. If the disruptive technology is irrelevant to them, the unit will keep serving its real demand system even while talking about the new effort.

The problem cannot be reduced to weak leadership or bad attitudes. An incumbent unit can be well-managed and still be the wrong home. The managers are solving for a customer base that rewards a different trajectory, so the disruptive project gets translated into forms that fit the old market or pushed aside when tradeoffs become real.

Executive intention therefore has limits. A directive from above can declare the project important, but it cannot by itself change which customers generate urgency inside the unit. The organization continues to answer to the market that pays for its legitimacy.

Christensen's response is targeted rather than theatrical. Separate or autonomous responsibility matters because it can relocate the project into a unit whose own customers need the technology. That creates a setting in which improvement, commitment, and judgment are pulled by the right market rather than by the incumbent trajectory.

The chapter's deepest warning is that rational neglect can emerge from competence. The wrong home does not have to reject the disruptive effort aggressively. It only has to keep serving the customers that matter more to it. That is enough to suffocate the initiative over time.

Chapter 6 stays disciplined by keeping the claim narrow. Right placement is necessary, but it is not the whole solution. Once the effort has the right customer base, later chapters still have to address scale, discovery, and capabilities.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The disruptive effort still needs a home if the old unit's customers do not want it. Christensen's answer is ruthless in its simplicity: give responsibility to the organization whose customers actually need the technology.

That works because organizations are governed by demand more than by declarations. Customers decide what feels urgent, what earns investment, and what counts as serious work. Put the disruptive effort inside a unit whose customers barely care, and the unit will keep honoring the people who pay for its status. The project stays alive just enough to be trimmed, delayed, and translated into old-market terms.

Goodwill is a weak defense. The incumbent team can be talented, disciplined, and verbally supportive. None of that changes the fact that its real incentives flow from a customer base pulling in another direction. The wrong home makes suffocation look like responsible prioritization.

Executive orders cannot fully break that pull. A leader can bless the project, but the owning unit still wakes up answering to the customers that already define its legitimacy. That demand system keeps winning the practical argument.

Autonomy matters only because it can move the center of gravity. A separate or autonomous unit can take the disruptive effort seriously when its own customers need the technology badly enough to make success matter. The move is about placing the work under a demand system that wants it alive.

The hard contradiction is that competence can still kill the future. The best-run incumbent unit may remain the worst place for the project simply because the wrong customers keep writing the rules.

The chapter does not claim structure solves everything. It claims customer-fit placement is the first non-negotiable. Once the effort has that, the next problem is whether the unit is small enough for the market to matter. Right home first. Right scale next.
